vectors.enisa_quote: all segments of the satellite lifecycle can be affected
vectors.reason: ENISA names no site; the control centre and ground design and development staff are implied by 'the victim' being a person who works on the lifecycle and by the ground assets listed, not by any quoted place.

vectors.enisa_quote: all segments of the satellite lifecycle can be affected
vectors.reason: Implied by 'all segments of the satellite lifecycle': manufacture and integration staff are victims too; the text does not name vendors or integrators.

vectors.enisa_quote: all segments of the satellite lifecycle can be affected
vectors.reason: Phishing reaches partner and vendor staff too, whose approved connections the mission trusts; ENISA names no partner or vendor, so the path is inferred from 'all segments'.

notes: EXF-0008 is analyst_added for the supply_chain vector: no source proposed a development-site exfiltration for TR53, and the supply_chain vector needs an outcome for 'gathering sensitive information'.

The RD-0002 reason now cites SPARTA's own description (spear-phishing of operators and vendors), not ENISA. IA-0009.01 stays dropped because the text names no collaborator.

review_response.finding: 'design and development' is not a ground-system site in attack_surface.json

fixed: enisa_quote 'launch of phishing or spear phishing' added to IA-0007 and IA-0009.02.

rows.enisa_quote: launch of phishing or spear phishing
rows.sparta_quote: Compromising the ground segment gives an adversary the most direct path to first execution against a spacecraft
rows.reason: A phished operator or contractor gives the adversary a foothold in the mission's ground systems; this is the route to the information-gathering outcome ENISA names.

rows.sparta_quote: The adversary resides in mission ground infrastructure and uses its trusted position to siphon data at scale
rows.reason: Gathering sensitive information is the outcome ENISA names; from a phished ground foothold the adversary siphons mission data.

rows.enisa_quote: launch of phishing or spear phishing
rows.sparta_quote: Vendors that design, integrate, or support mission systems often hold elevated, persistent routes into operations
rows.reason: ENISA says all lifecycle segments are affected, which includes suppliers and integrators; a phished vendor employee gives the attacker the vendor's own development and build environment, whereas the trusted_party vector rides the vendor's approved route into the mission.

rows.sparta_quote: the adversary gains access to source code, test vectors, telemetry captures, build artifacts, documentation, and configuration data
rows.reason: The development and integration environment is where 'gathering sensitive information' lands in the design, development and integration phases ENISA lists; no candidate source proposed an exfiltration for that side.

SPARTA's own description of compromising infrastructure lists 'spear-phishing of operators and vendors' as a way in, and ENISA names spear phishing; the compromised account or mailbox is the attacker resource used to reach the victim.
SPARTA names 'phishing an operator or contractor' as the typical path into a mission-operated ground system, the phishing ENISA states.
Mapping the people and roles around the mission finds the targets of spear phishing, whose victim is chosen by the attacker.
Inhibiting ground functionality is not described; ENISA states information gathering.
Presenting oneself as an authorized origin with insider credentials is identity takeover (TR43); TR53 states deception of the victim, not use of stolen identity.
Using safe mode to subvert protections is not described.
Using valid credentials to evade detection is identity-takeover behaviour (TR43), not stated for phishing.
Replaying command packets is not described; the phished victim acts, no packet is replayed.
Exploiting hardware design flaws is not described; phishing targets people.
Misusing hardware commands is not described.
Exploiting reduced protection in safe mode is not described.
Spoofing a signal to a receiver is TR54; TR53 deceives a person, not a receiver.
Replay of captured traffic is not described.
Intercepting the uplink is interception of communication (TR29); phishing does not reach the RF link.
Exfiltration through a payload channel is not described; ENISA names no channel.
Inserting malicious artifacts into delivered components is the supply chain compromise ENISA TR55 describes; TR53 names deception and information gathering, no insertion.
Tainting dependencies and development tools is the open-source compromise named in TR55; a phished developer is not described as altering them.
Delivering altered software is the supply chain compromise ENISA TR55 describes; TR53 states no software delivery.
Altering hardware before delivery is the third-party component compromise ENISA TR55 describes; TR53 states no change to hardware.
Compromise of a software-defined radio is not described; phishing targets people.
Reaching a satellite over a crosslink is not described; phishing targets staff.
A secondary or backup channel is not mentioned.
A backup ground station is not mentioned.
A receiver foothold is not mentioned.
Rendezvous and proximity operations are not described; phishing is remote.
Emanations collection is not described; phishing is by message.
Docked-vehicle access is not described.
Grappling a satellite is not described.
A hosted payload is not mentioned.
Tampering with the update pipeline is not described.
Sending valid-looking commands from a compromised ground system is the malicious commanding of TR52; TR53 states no commanding.
An outside RF transmitter is not described; the deception is aimed at people.
A rogue ground station is not described; the deception is aimed at people.
A rogue spacecraft is not described.
A counterspace weapon is not described.

Using a host spacecraft to reach a hosted payload is not described.

Altering settings while code stays intact is parameter modification (TR57); TR53 states no such change.
Falsifying or deleting data is data modification (TR39); TR53 states information gathering.
Blocking or redirecting commands and data is traffic manipulation (TR32); not stated in TR53.
Replacing firmware or logic is firmware corruption (TR42); not stated in TR53.

Moving into a hosted payload is not described.

Acquiring ground station equipment is not needed for phishing.
Obtaining cryptographic keys is not described.
Choosing a delivery mechanism in general terms does not say what phishing does; its description names no phishing.
Gathering spacecraft design information is not what spear phishing needs; ENISA mentions nothing about design.

Supply-chain information is not what ENISA's phishing targets.
